# Change and adjacency {#lagoa-change}

## Transitions between dates {-}

Knowing how much each class grew or shrank does not tell you where the area
went. `land_change()` answers that question by comparing the maps pixel by
pixel, at two or three dates, and measuring what stayed, what was converted and
into what:

```{r change, fig.height=6.5}
change <- land_change(maps, years = c(1985, 2024), language = "en")
change$plot
```

```{r include=FALSE}
im <- change$interval_metrics
cm <- change$class_metrics
f3 <- cm[cm$code == 3, ]
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
top <- cm[order(-cm$gross_change_ha), ][1:5, ]
tabela(data.frame(Class = top$class, `1985 (ha)` = top$initial_ha, `2024 (ha)` = top$final_ha,
                  `Gain (ha)` = top$gain_ha, `Loss (ha)` = top$loss_ha, `Net (ha)` = top$net_ha,
                  check.names = FALSE), 0)
```

Between 1985 and 2024, `r num(100 * im$change_fraction, 0)`% of the area changed
class. Almost all of that is quantity change (`r num(im$quantity_ha, 0)` ha),
meaning that one class grew by taking the place of another; only
`r num(im$allocation_ha, 0)` ha are swaps of position between classes. The forest
illustrates the picture well: only `r num(100 * f3$persistence_fraction, 0)`% of
the 1985 forest formation was still standing in 2024, and the
`r num(f3$gain_ha, 0)` ha that appeared elsewhere did not make up for the
`r num(f3$loss_ha, 0)` ha that were lost.

With `years = c(1985, 2004, 2024)`, the diagram gains a third column and shows
the trajectories across both intervals.

## Adjacency between classes {-}

`land_to_graph()` looks at neighbourhoods: it counts the contacts between pixels
of different classes and builds the landscape network, in which each node is a
class and the thickness of each link is the number of contacts between them.
With `weight = "boundary"`, the thickness becomes the boundary length in metres.

```{r network, fig.height=6.5}
network <- land_to_graph(maps, year = 2024, language = "en")
network$plot
```

```{r include=FALSE}
nm <- network$node_metrics
hub <- nm[which.max(nm$degree), ]
```

In 2024, the most connected class is `r tolower(hub$class)`, which borders
`r hub$degree` classes along `r num(hub$boundary_m / 1000, 1)` km of edges. The
tables `network$node_metrics` and `network$edge_metrics` detail degree,
strength, centrality and the length of each boundary.
